---
title: "Reactions in the atmosphere exercises"
---

Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

## 1. Reaction bookkeeping

Add the two chlorine steps in the notes. Identify the catalyst, the intermediate, and the net reaction.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Cancel species occurring on both sides of the summed equation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The net reaction is **O₃ + O → 2 O₂**. Cl is regenerated; ClO is the cycle intermediate. Neither appears in the net reaction.
:::

## 2. A supplied rate

Take k = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹ and constant OH = 1.0 × 10⁶ molecules/cm³. Calculate k′ and the lifetime in seconds and days. Use 86400 s/day.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Multiply k by OH; invert the resulting s⁻¹ value.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
k′ = **1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹**. The lifetime is **1.0 × 10⁶ s**, about **11.6 days** for this one constant sink. It is an e-folding time, not a half-life.
:::

## 3. Does the cycle make net ozone?

Sum the NO₂ photolysis, O₃ formation, and NO + O₃ reactions. Why can peroxy radicals change the outcome?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The third body and all nitrogen/oxygen intermediates cancel.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The basic cycle gives no net chemical change apart from energy conversion. A peroxy pathway can convert NO to NO₂ without using O₃, allowing the subsequent photolysis to contribute net ozone production.
:::

## 4. Location and evidence

An ozone measurement rises at a surface station. Can you infer increased stratospheric ozone or identify a single emission source? Explain what else is needed.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A measurement is local; production and transport both matter.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
No. Surface ozone depends on precursor chemistry, sunlight, deposition, mixing, and transported ozone. Altitude-resolved measurements, precursor observations, and meteorological information are needed. The molecular formula alone does not identify origin.
:::

## Explore: OH and the lifetime of a gas {#explore}

Predict what happens to the lifetime of gas X if the OH concentration doubles.
Then predict how far X can travel if its reaction with OH is 100 times slower.
Change one input at a time and keep apart the rate constant, the lifetime, and
the half-life.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/demo.css">
<div data-demo="lifetime" role="group" aria-label="OH-controlled lifetime of a gas">
<p>Reference case: k = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹ and OH = 1.0 × 10⁶ molecules/cm³ give k′ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹, a lifetime of 1.0 × 10⁶ s (11.6 days) and a half-life of 8.0 days.</p>
</div>
<script src="../demos/core.js"></script>
<script src="../demos/lifetime.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Choose **Worked example**, then **Twice as much OH**. By what factor did
k′, the lifetime and the half-life change? Check the new lifetime by hand.

**E2.** Choose **Slow reaction**. Compare the lifetime with the transport times
on the lecture slide. Why can a gas like this spread over the whole globe while
the worked-example gas stays a regional problem?

**E3.** Choose **Add deposition 0.1 per day**. Why is the new lifetime shorter
than both 11.6 days and 10 days? Explain why the two loss rate constants are
added, not the two lifetimes.

### Model conditions and hand check

For the worked example, k′ = k × [OH] = (1.0 × 10⁻¹²)(1.0 × 10⁶) =
**1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹**. The lifetime is 1/k′ = 1.0 × 10⁶ s, and dividing by
86400 s/day gives **11.6 days**. The half-life is 0.693 × 11.6 = **8.0 days**.
With twice as much OH, k′ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹ and the lifetime is **5.8 days**.
With deposition added, the loss rate constants add:
0.0864 + 0.100 = 0.186 per day, so the lifetime is 1/0.186 = **5.4 days**.

OH is held at one constant value, taken as an average over day and night. The
gas sits in one air parcel with no new emissions, so the amount left falls as
e^(−t/τ). The other loss is a simple first-order process, such as deposition,
given per day. The transport classes use the approximate times from the lecture:
about a day to mix the lowest air layer, a few weeks to circle a hemisphere, and
about a year to mix between hemispheres. Real OH varies with sunlight, season
and place, and k depends on temperature.
